Dr. Alex Rozov · Barzilai Medical Center
Decision support for clinicians — not a registered medical device
Good morning. I'm Alex Rozov — I'm a pulmonologist, and I head an internal medicine department here at Barzilai. For the next few minutes I want to show you a small tool I built for something we all do many times a day: reading a blood gas. It's called Acid-Base Scout. You take a photo of the gas results — on the patient's electronic record on the screen, or the analyser printout — and the app walks through the whole interpretation, not just the first line. It's in closed beta, it's free during the beta, and by the end of this talk you'll have the codes to install it on your own phone. One thing up front, and I'll come back to it: this is decision support. It is not a registered medical device, and it doesn't make decisions for you.

01Is the compensation what it should be?

Winter's formula gives the expected value — not a feeling.

02Is there a gap — after albumin?

Corrected for albumin, so a low albumin does not hide a HAGMA.

03Is a second process hiding?

The delta ratio unmasks the disorder behind the first one.

Let's start with what actually happens at the bedside. A gas comes back. We look at the pH, we look at the pCO₂, we name a disorder, and we move on. Most of the time that's fine. But the gas has more to say, and three questions tend to get skipped — especially at three in the morning. [click] First: is the compensation what it should be? Winter's formula gives you an expected pCO₂. If the measured value falls outside that range, there is a second, respiratory process. [click] Second: is there an anion gap — and is it still there after you correct for albumin? Our patients in internal medicine often have a low albumin, and every gram per decilitre below four hides about two and a half points of gap. [click] Third: is something hiding behind the first disorder? The delta ratio is how you find a metabolic alkalosis sitting under a ketoacidosis, or a normal-gap acidosis under a lactic one. None of this is difficult. It's just easy to skip. The app asks all three questions, every time.
What it does
Photograph the results. Get the whole reading.

Read

Photograph the gas on the patient's electronic record screen, or the analyser printout. The values fill in, and you confirm each one before anything is calculated.

Interpret

Primary disorder, expected compensation, anion gap, delta ratio, mixed disorders — and which tests to send next.

Explain

Every step shows its formula and threshold. Learn mode walks residents through the method.

So what does it do? Three things. [click] It reads. You photograph the blood gas results — straight off the patient's electronic record on the screen, or the analyser printout — and the values fill in on the phone. Then you check them — every one — before anything is calculated. [click] It interprets. Primary disorder, expected compensation, the anion gap corrected for albumin, the delta ratio, mixed disorders — and a short list of the tests that would sharpen the differential. [click] And it explains. Every number comes with its formula and its threshold, so you can see exactly why it said what it said — and argue with it if you disagree. There is also a Learn mode for students and residents. I'll show you that in a few minutes.

This is the whole workflow — four steps. [click] One: open a new patient. The app starts straight on the camera. [click] Two: photograph the results — the patient's electronic record on the screen, or the analyser printout. All the values in the frame, no glare. That is really the only skill involved. [click] Three: check the numbers. This is the step that matters most. The app reads well, but you are the one who confirms every value before anything is calculated. And if a test wasn't sent — say there's no lactate on this gas — you simply swipe that row away, so it isn't treated as a value. [click] Four: read the answer. The disorders, the compensation, and what to send next. From the photo to the answer is a matter of seconds.
Illustrative case · not a real patient
What a quick glance would miss
Young woman, type 1 diabetes, two days of vomiting.
pH 7.32 pCO2 32 HCO3− 16 Na+ 140 Cl− 92 K+ 3.1 glucose 480
AG = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−) = 140 − (92 + 16) = 32
High anion gap metabolic acidosis · Winter's: 1.5 × 16 + 8 = 32 ± 2 → compensation appropriate
ΔAG32 − 12 = 20
ΔHCO3−24 − 16 = 8
Δ ratio 2.5 → the gap rose far more than HCO3− fell: a concurrent metabolic alkalosis
SEND NEXT albumin osmolality β-hydroxybutyrate creatinine
Here is an illustrative case — not a real patient. A young woman with type 1 diabetes, two days of vomiting. pH 7.32, pCO₂ 32, bicarbonate 16, sodium 140, chloride 92, glucose 480. At a glance: a mild metabolic acidosis, it's DKA, done. Let's read it to the end. [click] The anion gap: 140 minus 92 plus 16 — that's 32. A high anion gap metabolic acidosis, as expected. Winter's formula: one and a half times 16, plus 8, is 32, plus or minus 2. The measured pCO₂ is 32, so the respiratory compensation is appropriate. [click] Now the delta ratio. The gap went up by 20 — from 12 to 32. The bicarbonate went down by only 8 — from 24 to 16. Twenty over eight is 2.5. When the gap rises much more than the bicarbonate falls, something has been adding bicarbonate back. Here, it's two days of vomiting. So this is two disorders: a ketoacidosis and a metabolic alkalosis. That is why the pH looks milder than the illness — and it changes how you think about her potassium and chloride. [click] And the app lists what to send next to sharpen the picture: albumin, osmolality, beta-hydroxybutyrate, creatinine. [click] And this is what the app shows on the phone: a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, appropriate compensation, and the concurrent metabolic alkalosis — the same reading we just did by hand, in a few seconds.
Nothing hidden
Every number shows its working
Formulas, thresholds and references sit next to each result — so the reasoning can be checked, taught and argued with.
  • Corrected anion gap, expected pCO2 and delta ratio, with their inputs
  • Add albumin, osmolality, β-OHB or creatinine and the reading updates
  • Learn mode: the method, step by step, for residents and students
AG = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−)
pCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3− + 8 ± 2
Δ ratio = ΔAG ÷ ΔHCO3−
I didn't want a black box. Every result in the app shows its working: the formula, the inputs that went into it, and the threshold it was compared against. If the app says the compensation is appropriate, you can open it and see the expected range it calculated. [click] On the left: optional tests. If you add albumin, osmolality, beta-hydroxybutyrate or creatinine, the reading updates — the gap is corrected for albumin, an osmolar gap appears, and so on. [click] On the right: the method itself, written out as formulas. This is useful on teaching rounds. The reasoning is on the screen, and you can discuss it with the team.

  • pCO2 stays hidden until you have predicted it
  • Type the numbers: anion gap, delta ratio, osmolar and urine gaps
  • Graded by the same engine as the clinical side
  • Progress shows what to work on; nothing touches patient data
Learn is a separate mode inside the same app. The header turns green and says "Learning — not a patient", so a teaching case can never be confused with a real one, and nothing from Learn ever touches the patient side. There are 343 teaching cases across 106 patterns — from plain DKA to toxic alcohols, renal tubular acidosis and triple disorders — in three levels of difficulty. They are synthetic, composite cases with no real patient data, and I have reviewed every one of them. [click] The student works step by step. First: what is the primary disorder? Notice that the pCO₂ is hidden. [click] Then: what pCO₂ would you expect? They type a number — and only after that is the measured pCO₂ revealed. Hiding it is the whole point; otherwise you just read it off the screen. After that come the anion gap, the delta ratio, the osmolar and urine gaps where they apply — typed numbers, not multiple choice. The answer key is the engine itself — the same engine that reads real gases — so what students are taught and what the clinical side says can never disagree. [click] Progress stays on the phone and tells the student which steps they keep getting wrong and what to work on next. It works well for students and interns in a quiet moment on call.

Only the cropped strip of values is sent — not the patient label.
One more feature — optional, and still in testing: Cloud check. The phone reads the photo on its own, on the device. If Cloud check is on, the strip with the values is also read a second time in the cloud, and the two readings are compared, value by value. Where they agree — fine. Where they differ, the value is highlighted, and you look at the photo and decide. And sometimes the cloud picks up a value the phone missed; it's offered to you for review. Only the cropped strip with the numbers is sent — not the patient label. [click] This is how it looks in the app. It doesn't replace your own check of the numbers. It points you to the ones worth a second look.
Please read
Decision support — not a registered medical device.

The clinician confirms every value and makes every decision.

Calculations run on the phone. Cloud check, when used, sends only the strip of values.

Closed beta: if something looks wrong, report it — that is what the beta is for.

I want to be very clear about this slide. Acid-Base Scout is decision support. It is not a registered medical device. The clinician confirms every value and makes every decision. The app supports your reasoning — it doesn't replace it, and please don't use it as the only basis for a treatment decision. The calculations run on the phone. The only thing that leaves the phone — and only if you use Cloud check — is the strip with the values. And this is a closed beta. If you see anything that looks wrong — a misread value, an interpretation, even a confusing word — please tell me. That is exactly what the beta is for, and fixes go out quickly.

Here is what this looks like on the screen. These are example values — yours will be different. When you first open the app, it shows a screen called "Unlock this device", with your Device ID in large letters and a Copy button. Copy it. [click] Now on the site, scroll to "No invite code? Get one here". There are three lines: your name, your email, and the event word — BARZILAI2026. Tap "Get my invite code", and the code appears right below, starting with TRIAL. If you ever lose it, enter the same email again and the same code comes back. [click] Just above, in "Get your key", the invite code is already filled in for you. Paste the Device ID into the first line and tap "Get the key". The key appears below — four groups of four characters. [click] Copy the key, go back to the app, paste it into the empty line under the Device ID, and tap Unlock. That's it — the app opens. The key only works on that one phone, and each invite code unlocks one phone. If you lose the key, ask again with the same Device ID and invite code and you get the same key. But if you delete and reinstall the app, it gets a new Device ID — so please don't reinstall; update over the top instead. If it happens anyway, write to me and I'll sort it out.
